t: Dinner's ready, buddy.
Your mom's voice comes from the kitchen.
You're on the living room floor, reaching behind the couch for your phone charger.
You say what you always say.
One minute. Your hand goes through the wall, not into it.
Through it, the wall feels like cold water for a second.
Then the floor disappears and you fall about a meter onto something soft and damp.
You open your eyes and your whole world is yellow.
Yellow wallpaper. Yellow carpet that smells like an old sponge, a ceiling of flickering lights,
humming one long, flat note.
A hallway turns left, then right, then left.
No windows, no doors, no end.
You look at your phone. 6.42 p.m., no signal.
You check again 20 minutes later, still 6.42.
Here's what you don't know yet.
You're about to spend a hundred days in this place.
You'll lose count of the days.
You'll hear your mom call you for dinner from the end of an empty hallway.
You'll find a stranger who has been here for three years.
And on day 100, you'll stand in front of the only door out and you'll realize you have to decide
who gets to leave first.
And when you finally get home, your mom will still be calling you to dinner.
Day one, you walk, you shout, nothing answers.
The hum swallows your voice after about three seconds.
There's a strange thing about that hum.
The lights flicker very fast, much faster than your eyes can see.
In most countries, the electricity in the wall changes direction 50 or 60 times a second.
A fluorescent tube lights up and dims on every change.
So it flickers 100 or 120 times every second.
Your brain doesn't notice, but after a few hours you start to feel it.
Dull headache, tight jaw, tired eyes.
By evening, you're thirsty.
Here's the rule you learned in school and now it's the only one that matters.
A person can live about three weeks without food, but without water, about three days.
Day two, you walk faster.
Hallway after hallway, every turn looks identical.
The same stain, the same smell, the same hum.
By lunchtime, your mouth feels like sandpaper.
By evening, your lips crack.
Day three, your hands shake and you find it.
A tiny room about the size of a closet.
On the floor, a row of plastic bottles with no labels.
You unscrew one with shaking fingers.
The water inside is clear and cold and it tastes faintly of almonds.
You drink the whole bottle.
Then you sit on the carpet and cry.
Whatever this place is, it wants you alive, which is almost worse.
You carry five bottles with you.
You write on the wall with a pen from your pocket.
Water, room 14, because here's another rule you learn fast.
If you don't mark where you've been, every hallway becomes the same hallway.
Day nine, you can't sleep.
The lights never turn off. There's no night and the human body has a clock inside it.
Scientists found out how strong it is in 1962.
A French researcher named Michel Sifra spent two months alone in a cave
with no sun, no clock and no calendar.
When his team called to tell him his time was up, he thought it was only the middle of the experiment.
He was off by nearly a month.
Without daylight, his body kept sleeping and waking on its own schedule a little longer
than 24 hours, and his mind kept losing days.
That's what happens to you too.
You sleep when you can't stay awake anymore.
You wake when your stomach tells you.
You stop knowing if it's morning or if you've slept for two hours or 12.
You try counting your sleeps on the wall, one scratch per sleep.
But some sleeps are short and some are long and some stays you can't remember if you scratched or not.
On day 16, you start seeing things, faces in the wallpaper, shapes at the edge of the hallway
that vanish when you turn. It isn't magic and it isn't ghosts.
When your eyes stare at one flat, empty color for long enough, the brain gets desperate
for something to look at, so it invents it.
Scientists call it the Gansfeld effect.
Even healthy people start to hallucinate after a few hours.
You've had weeks.
By day 18, you've stopped talking to yourself.
By day 23, you've started talking to the carpet.
By day 30, you can recite your mom's lasagna recipe from memory, just so you remember
what a real kitchen smells like.
You tell the wallpaper about your little brother, Noah, who still sleeps with the hall light on.
You tell it about school.
You tell it about the dumb argument you had with your mom last Tuesday.
About the dishes. You'd give anything to have that argument again.
Day 40, you're sitting on the floor in a long hallway when you hear it.
A voice far away from around the corner.
Dinner's ready. Your heart stops.
It's your mom, the exact voice.
The exact tone, a little tired, a little sing song.
The way she says it every night, you jump up.
You run toward it, tripping, shouting, mom, mom!
Around the corner, there's an empty hallway and again from the other end.
Dinner's ready. You stop.
Your legs are shaking. You look down the hall.
Nothing there. Then the voice comes again.
From right behind your shoulder, so close you can feel the breath.
Dinner's ready. And it stops, right where the last word should be.
It's the same voice, the same tone, even the same tiny breath she takes before she says it.
But the voice never says, buddy.
It never gets to the end.
It's like a recording of your mom with the most important part cut out.
Whatever is out there copied what you heard right before you fell, perfectly.
But it doesn't know the word that only she says.
You back away. You don't run.
You walk slowly, quietly, the way you'd walk away from a dog that might bite.
The voice follows for a long time, repeating the same two words, getting softer and softer.
When it finally stops, you realize you've been holding your breath for almost a minute.
That night, you don't sleep.
For the first time since you fell, you're afraid of the hum instead of annoyed by it
because the hum might hide something else.
Day 52, you find the chalk.
At first, it's just a single line, low on a wall, a white tally mark, then two.
Then a whole column of them, hundreds, neat bundles of five, marching down the hallway.
And at the end of the column, there's a hand-drawn arrow and under it a single word.
Hi.
You run following the arrow.
Around five corners, you find a small room made of stacked cardboard boxes,
a blanket, a tiny pile of water bottles, and sitting in the corner hugging her knees,
a girl about your age, dirty hoodie, tangled hair, a piece of white chalk in her hand.
She stares at you for a long time.
When she finally speaks, her voice is cracked, like it's been years since she used it.
You're real?
I think so. She laughs and then she cries and then she laughs again.
Her name is Iris. She tells you she's been here for 1,094 days.
Three years, give or take.
She counted everyone with chalk, even the days she was sure she'd lost.
She's 15. She was 15 when she fell.
She says it like she's still not sure it's true.
How is that possible, you ask?
I've been here 50 days.
She shows you her phone. The screen says 317 a.m.
She turns it on every single day.
And every single day, it says 317.
Time doesn't work right here, she says it's slow.
It's really, really slow. I think out there, it hasn't even been a day.
For the first time in 52 days, you let yourself believe it.
Your mom doesn't know you're gone.
She's still standing in the kitchen, waiting for her son to come to dinner.
It's only been a few seconds.
Iris teaches you everything she's learned.
Don't walk in straight lines.
The place bends if you do.
Don't whistle. The voice thing likes whistling.
Never follow a sound you recognize.
Only follow ones you don't.
And stay close to the chalk.
Over the next weeks, you learn about each other.
She had a little brother, too.
Leo, eight years old.
She was walking him home from school when she reached for a dropped glove behind a vending machine.
She says she hears him laugh sometimes down the hallways and she's learned not to follow it.
Some nights, you both sit on the floor and pretend to make dinner.
You cook lasagna out of nothing, layer by layer from memory, arguing about how much cheese is enough.
She says more. You say less.
Neither of you wins.
For the next 40 days, you explore together.
You map the hallways on the back of a cardboard box.
You build a bigger and bigger drawing with arrows and symbols and little notes.
The first time you play a game of tic-tac-toe on the wall, Iris laughs so hard she has to sit down.
You find out something the loneliest people already know.
100 days alone is a lot harder than 100 days with one other person.
100 days together is practically a vacation.
Day 70, she shows you the map she's been making for three years.
Most of it is crossed out, dead ends, loops.
One section deep in the left side is circled in red.
This is the only place I haven't gone, she says.
I'm scared. Why?
Because the last time I heard my brother, you understand, neither of you talks for a while.
Day 98, you go together.
The hallway starts to change.
The carpet gets thinner, the lights get brighter, the hum gets quieter, and then stops.
For the first time in 98 days, there's silence and it feels so strange you wanna scream.
At the end of the hall, there's a door, plain white with a normal silver handle.
A door like you'd find in any house.
A thin line of warm light glows along the bottom and from the other side, very faintly,
you can smell something that makes you wanna fall to your knees.
Dishwasher soap, lasagna, carpet that's actually clean.
Next to the door, there's a lever, a big iron one, taller than you, bolted into the wall.
It's sticky with old dust.
At the top, someone has scratched a tiny message into the metal, in handwriting that isn't irises.
Hold it down, door opens, let go, door closes.
Virus reads it three times.
Then she sits down very slowly on the carpet.
That's why nobody gets out, she says.
Somebody has to hold the lever and whoever holds it can't go through.
You look at the door, you look at the lever, you look at her.
One person goes, she says, one person stays.
We'll figure it out.
No, she shakes her head, she's smiling, but her hands are shaking.
I've had three years to figure it out.
You go, your mom's waiting, your brother's waiting, go.
I'm not leaving you. You have to.
No. You walk to the lever, you wrap both hands around it
and push down with your whole body.
The door clicks open.
Warm light spills into the hall and through the crack, you can hear it.
The clink of a fork, the hum of a refrigerator, someone coughing softly in another room.
You turn to Iris, go through, what?
You've been here three years, you go.
I'll hold it. She stares at you.
Then she stands up and for the first time in three years, she walks toward the door.
And right before she steps through, she stops.
She turns around and she says something that nobody had said to you in a hundred days.
Don't hold it, pull it.
You don't understand. Look at the lever, she says.
It's built so someone can hold it down from the other side too.
And that's when you see it. On the back of the door, bolted to the frame
is a second lever, smaller, rusty, facing the other way and the engraving beneath it
in the same careful handwriting.
If you go through, turn around.
Every single person who ever escaped this place
walked through that door and never once looked back.
Iris steps through the door, you hear her gasp.
Then you hear her cry out, a wild, crazy, happy shout and the sound of her running.
And then she comes back. She appears in the doorway, tears all over her face,
holding the outer lever with both hands.
Go, she says, I've got it, go home.
You let go of the lever on your side.
You step through the door and Iris lets go behind you.
The door clicks shut.
When you turn around, it's just a wall and you're standing behind your living room couch.
The light is the warm light of your house.
The air smells like lasagna.
Your phone is in your hand. You look at the screen.
6.43 PM, Iris is standing next to you, shaking, laughing, crying all at once.
You're both still holding hands.
You both have dirty hair, ragged clothes and thinner arms than you remember.
You've been gone for a hundred days.
Your mom has been waiting for one minute.
On the table, in the kitchen, there's a plate with your name on it.
You look at Iris, she looks at you and neither of you says a word because there's nothing you can say.
So would you have gone back for someone you barely knew?
If you were Iris, would you have let him go through first?
Tell us in the comments.
And just when you think it's over, you hear it.
From the kitchen, your mom's voice.
Dinner's ready, buddy.
And from somewhere inside the wall behind you, soft and perfectly in sync, you hear it again.
Dinner's ready. Then for the first time ever, it finishes the sentence.
Buddy, hit like and subscribe for part two.
